t.2.41.1: Then Rāghava, having reached the delightful bank of the Tamasā, looked at Sītā and spoke these words to Saumitri.
t.2.41.2: This night today, O Saumitri, is the first of our dwelling in the forest, begun as we set out for the woods. Good fortune to you! So you ought not to be filled with longing.
t.2.41.3: Look at the desolate forests all around, which seem to weep, now that the beasts and birds have come back each to its own shelter and lie hidden there.
t.2.41.4: Today the city of Ayodhyā, the royal capital of my father, will surely grieve, with all its women and men, for us who have gone away; of this there is no doubt.
t.2.41.5: Bharata, whose soul is devoted to dharma, will surely console my father and my mother with words in keeping with dharma, artha and kāma.
t.2.41.6: Reflecting again and again on Bharata's kindness, I do not grieve for my father, nor for my mother either, O Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.41.7: O tiger among men, by following me you have done what needed to be done, for help had to be found for the protection of Vaidehī.
t.2.41.8: But tonight, O Saumitri, I shall pass this night on water alone; for this is what pleases me, even though forest food of many kinds is at hand.
t.2.41.9: Having spoken thus to Saumitra, Rāghava then said to Sumantra as well, "Be watchful over the horses, gentle one."
t.2.41.10: When the sun had set, Sumantra unyoked the horses, gave them plenty of fodder, and stayed close at hand.
t.2.41.11: "Let him worship the auspicious evening twilight": seeing that night had come, the charioteer, together with Saumitri, prepared a bed for Rāma.
t.2.41.12: Seeing that bed made of the leaves of trees on the bank of the Tamasā, Rāma, together with his wife and with Saumitri, lay down upon it.
t.2.41.13: Seeing his brother sound asleep together with his wife, Lakṣmaṇa recounted to the charioteer the many virtues of Rāma.
t.2.41.14: As Saumitri stayed awake that whole night on the bank of the Tamasā, telling the charioteer of Rāma's virtues, the sun rose.
t.2.41.16: Rising up and observing those subjects, the greatly illustrious Rāma spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, who bore auspicious marks.
t.2.41.15: There, at some distance from the Tamasā, whose banks were crowded with herds of cattle, Rāma spent that night together with his subjects.
t.2.41.17: O Saumitri, Lakṣmaṇa, look now at these people who care only for us, indifferent even to their own homes, lying asleep at the roots of trees.
t.2.41.19: But while they are fast asleep, let us quickly mount the chariot and go along a road where there is no danger from any quarter.
t.2.41.18: Judging by the vow these citizens are making to bring me back, they would cast away even their lives, but they will never give up their resolve.
t.2.41.20: Therefore, from now on, let the dwellers of the Ikṣvāku city, devoted to me, no longer sleep again taking shelter at the roots of trees.
t.2.41.21: For the citizens must be freed by the sons of kings from sorrow brought about by themselves; the dwellers of the city must surely never be yoked to sorrow by the king's sons themselves.
t.2.41.22: Lakṣmaṇa said to Rāma, who stood there like Dharma itself in visible form: "It pleases me, O greatly wise one; let it be boarded quickly."
t.2.41.23: Then the charioteer, making great haste, yoked the chariot with those excellent horses, and with hands joined in reverence he announced to Rāma that it was ready.
t.2.41.24: But in order to mislead the citizens, Rāma spoke these words to the charioteer: "Mount the chariot, O charioteer, and drive off facing north."
t.2.41.25: Drive swiftly onward for a moment, then turn the chariot back again. Act with care, so that the citizens may not know where I have gone.
t.2.41.26: Having heard Rāma's words, the charioteer did as he was told, and returning, he reported the chariot to Rāma.
t.2.41.27: Mounting that chariot, Rāghava, together with his retinue, crossed the river Tamasā, swift-flowing and full of turbulent whirlpools.
t.2.41.28: Having crossed over, the glorious, mighty-armed one reached the great highway, auspicious and free of thorns, a place without fear for those who see danger everywhere.
t.2.41.29: When the night had given way to dawn, those citizens, bereft of Rāghava, were struck down by grief and became motionless, their minds stunned.
t.2.41.30: Wasted by tears born of grief, looking about here and there, the sorrowful ones could not see even a glimpse of Rāma.
t.2.41.31: Then, having gone on a little while longer by following the track, he was overwhelmed by great despair when the track was lost.
t.2.41.32: Because the track of the chariot was lost, the high-minded citizens turned back, saying, "What is this? What shall we do? We have been struck down by fate."
t.2.41.33: Then, weary in mind, they all went back by the very road by which they had come, to Ayodhyā, the city whose good people were stricken with grief.
